startMessages: Monday, 7:58 AM. Your first week on the Millhaven police force. Sergeant Prakash is at the front desk, and he wants to see you.

The front desk of the Millhaven Police Department. Sergeant Prakash sits behind the counter with two wire trays and a desk radio. A bulletin board and a filing cabinet stand against the left wall, and a doorway marked RECORDS leads north. The front doors are behind you, to the south.
Sergeant Prakash has twenty-two years on the force. He reads every form twice: once for the facts and once for the spelling.
You'd have to shout. Walk up to the front desk.
Prakash: "Reyes. Good, you're early. Hollis Pharmacy on Main Street was broken into overnight. Back window smashed, prescription painkillers gone."

Prakash: "A Quickstep Delivery driver, Marty Kowal, called it in at 6:10 this morning. Says he found the window on his morning drop and saw some kids running off. He's waiting by his van on Main Street."
Prakash: "Take his statement, document the scene, and bring me a report I can hand to the prosecutor. Here's the form." He hands you a blank case report.
Prakash: "And take the camera off the filing cabinet. Evidence you can't show me didn't happen."
Prakash: "I hear you made an arrest. Good. Now the paperwork, Reyes. Give me that report."
Prakash: "Warehouse 9 on Pier Road. Bukowski is parked out there. Radio for backup before you go in. That is not a suggestion."
Prakash: "You've got a timeline problem and a sticker off a crate. Records keeps the property ledger, north down the hall. Find out who rents what."
Prakash: "Kowal is on Main Street by his van, and Hollis Pharmacy is next door. Listen to the first. Photograph the second."
Prakash: "You haven't checked Kowal's story yet. Drivers keep a delivery manifest. Ask to see it."
Prakash: "The pharmacy scene isn't documented. I want photographs and physical evidence."
Prakash: "The camera is still on the filing cabinet, Reyes. It won't walk to the pharmacy by itself."
Prakash: "Go home, Reyes. Come back tomorrow and do it again."

The bulletin board holds a softball sign-up sheet, a lost-cat flyer, a WANTED poster for a man who steals garden gnomes, and the duty roster. Your name is on the roster, in pencil. A blank index card is pinned in the middle.
The index card in the middle of the board now reads: HOLLIS PHARMACY, 12 MAIN ST. BREAK-IN OVERNIGHT. REPORTED 6:10 AM BY M. KOWAL, QUICKSTEP DELIVERY, VAN 14. OFFICER: REYES.
A gray filing cabinet. The department camera sits on top of it, next to a coffee ring.
A gray filing cabinet with a coffee ring on top.
The drawers are full of old parking tickets. Nothing you need.
You already have the camera.
Walk over to the filing cabinet first.
You take the department camera and check the counter. Twenty-four exposures left.
The department camera. It has a flash and twenty-four exposures left.
You need a camera for that.
Nothing here belongs in the case file. Save the film for the scene.
Prakash: "Don't."
Two wire trays sit on the counter. The gray one is labeled IN. The red one is labeled WRONG TRAY, and it is half full.
You don't have a report.
Walk up to the front desk first.
You drop the report in a tray. Prakash fishes it out without looking up. "Wrong tray, Reyes. Reports come to me, by hand. Give it here."
Prakash reads the report once for the facts and once for the spelling.
Prakash: "Timeline from the manifest. Photographs and a bottle from Hollis. The lease on Warehouse 9. An arrest with backup on scene." He stamps the report. "That'll stick. Good work, Reyes."
He drops the report in the IN tray. Your first case is closed and your first shift is over. Bud Bukowski owes you a coffee, and he is already telling everyone how it went.
Prakash reads the report and hands it back. "It's got holes, Reyes."
Prakash: "Kowal's statement hasn't been checked against anything."
Prakash: "No photographs or physical evidence from the pharmacy."
Prakash: "Nothing ties this to a location. Where did the stock go?"
Prakash: "And there's no arrest. A report needs an ending."
Prakash: "Already filed. Go home, Reyes."
You don't have a report yet. Talk to Sergeant Prakash.
Millhaven PD badge number 417. It's still shiny.
Your shoulder radio, tuned to Dispatch.
Dispatch: "Morning, Reyes. The sergeant is looking for you. He's at the front desk, same as always."
Dispatch: "Reminder, Reyes: Hollis Pharmacy, 12 Main Street. The driver is Marty Kowal, Quickstep Delivery, van 14."
Dispatch: "Backup to the front desk? Request denied, Reyes."
The front desk is chipped oak with a brass plate: SGT. PRAKASH. A desk radio sits by the trays, and its call light blinks now and then.
Through the window you can see the red brick of the hardware store across Main Street.
The clock reads a few minutes past eight.
A wooden bench for visitors. Someone has carved B.B. WAS HERE into the armrest.
No time to sit. It's your first week.
The doorway marked RECORDS leads north to the records office and the dispatch desk.
The front doors are behind you, to the south. Main Street is outside.
Officer Dana Reyes. Navy uniform, cap, duty belt and badge 417. First week on the job.
Bud Bukowski, your partner, is out on patrol. Prakash says you'll hear him before you see him.
Prakash: "Reyes! Where are you going? Your assignment is over here."
You see nothing unusual about that.
The only coffee here is a dry ring on top of the filing cabinet.
Green walls, gray tile and fluorescent lights. The precinct smells of toner and old coffee.
Kowal is waiting by his van on Main Street, south through the front doors.
Hollis Pharmacy is on Main Street, south through the front doors.
You haven't gotten that far yet.
The case report. Prakash will want every box filled in before you give it to him.
You can't take that.

startMessages: Millhaven Police, front desk. Sergeant Prakash sits behind the counter under the green office lights. A bulletin board hangs beside the Records door, and the street door is behind you.
Monday, 7:02 AM. Your first week on the Millhaven force. You have your badge and your radio. Sergeant Prakash looks up from his forms as you come in.

Prakash: "Reyes. Good. Hollis Pharmacy on Main Street was broken into overnight. A delivery driver, Tommy Vance from Quayside Freight, called it in at 6:10. Says he found the back door open on his route."
Prakash: "Here's the case file, and a camera. Talk to the driver, document the scene, collect what you can. Bud's already out on Main Street with Vance. Try not to let him talk the witness to sleep."
Prakash hands you the case file and a camera.
Prakash: "Driver is Tommy Vance, Quayside Freight. He's by his van on Main Street, next to the pharmacy. Records is down the hall if you need delivery logs. The board has the rest."
Sergeant Prakash has worked this desk for nineteen years. His mustache is going gray, and his coffee mug says WORLD'S OKAYEST SERGEANT.
Shift notices, a lost cat flyer and a softball sign-up sheet with one name on it: Bukowski.
A new card is pinned at the center of the board: HOLLIS PHARMACY, 14 MAIN ST. BREAK-IN, REPORTED 6:10 AM BY T. VANCE, QUAYSIDE FREIGHT. DELIVERY LOGS: RECORDS OFFICE.
Two wire trays sit on the desk. One is labeled IN. The other is labeled FILED IN WRONG TRAY.
Prakash: "Left tray is for forms. Right tray is for forms that went in the wrong tray. You'll use both before the week is out."
A wide laminate counter with a brass nameplate: SGT. R. PRAKASH. A radio sits at one end, its light blinking now and then.
The desk radio blinks each time dispatch keys the channel. Your own radio is on your belt.
Dispatch: "Dispatch here, Reyes. You're still in the building. The sergeant is about eight feet in front of you."
Dispatch: "Dispatch. Hollis Pharmacy, 14 Main Street. Complainant is Tommy Vance, Quayside Freight. He's waiting by his van. Bukowski is with him."
Millhaven Police badge number 417. It still looks new.
Prakash: "I issued it to you on Friday, Reyes. I remember what it looks like."
Prakash: "Ask first, Reyes. Then take."

Hollis Pharmacy break-in. Complainant: Tommy Vance, Quayside Freight driver, reported 6:10 AM. Back door found open. Assigned: Officer D. Reyes. Prakash has written BE THOROUGH across the top and underlined it twice.
A department camera. It takes decent pictures of doors, footprints and anything else that stands still.
You pour a cup from the machine. It tastes like it was made yesterday, which it probably was.
A dented steel coffee machine. Someone has taped a note to it: DO NOT KICK.
A gray filing cabinet, locked. The real files are in Records, down the hall.
The door to the Records Office. Delivery logs and lease records are kept there.
A faded WANTED poster for a man who stole twelve garden gnomes in 1987. Nobody has taken it down.
Prakash: "Reyes. Assignment first, then the street."
Prakash: "You don't have a case yet, Reyes. Or a report. Those come in that order."
Prakash: "Paperwork comes after the arrest, Reyes. Go work the case."
Prakash: "Morning, Reyes. Come over here. I've got something for you."
Prakash: "Morning. You have an assignment. Main Street is out the front door."
Bud is out on Main Street with the driver. Prakash says he could talk for a living.
Prakash glances up. "If you're stuck, Reyes, talk to me, read the board or call dispatch."
Prakash is waiting to give you an assignment. Talk to him.
Prakash: "Talk to the driver on Main Street, document the pharmacy, and check Records for delivery logs. Dispatch will repeat the details if you radio in."
You'll need to be closer to the counter for that.
There's nothing here worth photographing. The pharmacy is another matter.
The driver, the pharmacy and the evidence are all out on Main Street.

The duty board lists Ellis Vale's claimed 9 PM pharmacy delivery. The records office is west of this desk. The street and pharmacy are to the east.
Your badge says D. REYES, MILLHAVEN POLICE. The photograph looks more rested than you feel.
The police radio is tuned to dispatch. You can call dispatch about the driver after checking the records.
Dispatch answers: 'Check the delivery ledger first, Reyes. I can compare it with the route log.'
Dispatch repeats the route log. Vale's van was on Pier Road at nine, not at the pharmacy. You should check the pharmacy and preserve what you find there.
Prakash scans the report. 'Not yet. I need the driver's discrepancy, pharmacy evidence, a warehouse connection, and a supported arrest. Nothing in that list is optional.'
Prakash reads the complete report, signs it, and places it in the correct tray. 'Good work, Reyes. Go home before anyone finds another form.' Your first shift is over.
The desk holds Prakash's folder, a radio console and a tray of forms. Prakash insists that the tray for completed forms really is different.
The notice board lists the incident and Ellis Vale's delivery claim. Talk to Prakash for the assignment, read the board, or walk west to records and east to the street.
Prakash waits for you to finish the case. You can ask him for a reminder or file the report once the arrest is made.
You already have your badge and radio. The folder stays at the desk so Prakash can keep a copy.
The pharmacy lies across the street. Prakash wants the driver's route checked and the break-in documented.
The report needs evidence and an arrest before Prakash will sign it.
The radio gives a short burst of static. Dispatch needs a specific question: call dispatch.
Prakash's form tray is where complete reports go, not loose evidence.
The station clock reads a little after nine. Vale's claimed delivery was at nine sharp.
Prakash says, 'One step at a time. Read the board, check the ledger in records, then visit the pharmacy. If you need me, come back.'
The records hall is west; the street is east. Prakash remains at his desk.

startMessages: Thornwall's gate stands open across the drawbridge. The Great Hall lies beyond it, and the king is waiting. A royal notice is posted by the moat, bread sits on the bench and a lantern burns on its hook. The path east runs into the meadow.
Castle Thornwall stands across the moat, gray and patched. The drawbridge leads into the Great Hall. A notice is posted by the moat, and the path runs east into the meadow.
Bread waits on the bench.
A lantern burns on a hook by the path.

BY ORDER OF KING BRANNOC OF THORNWALL:
The squire Wenna will report to the Great Hall at once. She should bring bread for the road and a light to see by.
Please do not swim in the moat. It upsets Duchess.
The notice is pinned there for everyone to read. You leave it where it is.
You pick up the bread. It is still warm, and the cook has wrapped it in a soft cloth. The cloth smells of brass polish.
You need to get closer to the bench.
A round loaf in a basket, left on the bench for your journey.
You lift the lantern off its hook. It is brass under the soot, and the flame burns steadily.
You need to get closer to the lantern post.
A brass lantern hangs from the hook, lit and dull with soot.
An alligator floats in the moat with only its eyes and snout above the water. It watches you in the patient way of something that is never in a hurry.
The alligator says nothing. It gives the impression of listening, and of thinking about lunch.
The alligator ignores the bread. It prefers food that walks in on its own.
You step to the edge of the moat. Two yellow eyes turn toward you and the water goes very still. Swimming here would be a bad idea.
You jump into the moat anyway. Duchess the alligator reaches you before the ripples do. The notice did ask you not to upset her.
The moat is dark and deep, and an alligator drifts through it as if it owns the place. It probably does.
Castle Thornwall is gray and drafty, and smaller than it was in your grandmother's day. The kingdom's last lit candle burns somewhere inside.
The gate stands open. Deep inside the Great Hall a single candle flickers. The king will be near it.
The drawbridge is lowered across the moat. Its planks creak, but they hold.
The path curls east around the moat and into the meadow. Out in the countryside there is a river, a hut with a smoking chimney and an old oak, if the stories are right.
Far beyond the hills, smoke rises from a crooked chimney. Someone out there keeps a fire going day and night.
A plain wooden bench by the moat. Someone has left bread on it for you.
A plain wooden bench by the moat.

startMessages: Morning at the gate of Thornwall. The castle has seen better centuries. A notice is pinned to a board by the road, and something in the moat is watching you.

The gray walls of Thornwall rise beyond the moat. A drawbridge leads to the great hall. A notice board stands by the road, the cook has left something on the stump, and the road runs east into the meadow.

BY ORDER OF KING BRANNOC. The last candle in Thornwall is burning low. Wanted: a squire to recover the Three Bright Things - the Bell that sank in the river gorge, the Ember that never goes out, and the Map that will not stay in one place. Sign below. Bread and lantern provided.
A quill hangs from a string beside the notice. You write WENNA under the king's seal. It is the only name on the page. The errand is yours.
Your name is already there, larger than you meant to write it.
The notice is meant for every squire to read. Sign it first, and then it is yours.
You unpin the notice, fold it and tuck it into your sleeve. The sleeve has room for several more.
You already have it.
A round loaf sits in a basket on the stump, with a note from the cook: FOR THE ROAD.
A round brown loaf, baked this morning. It still smells of the oven.
You take the loaf of bread. The cook's note says FOR THE ROAD, so it must be yours.
You need to be closer.
You lift the lantern from its hook. The flame inside is small and steady.
A brass lantern hangs from a hook on the post. It is already lit.
A small brass lantern. Its flame burns steadily, even when you swing it.
The lantern is already lit.
An alligator floats in the moat with only its eyes and snout above the water. A sign on the bank reads: PLEASE DO NOT FEED DUNSTAN.
You say good morning to Dunstan. Dunstan blinks once, slowly, and says nothing.
The sign asks you not to feed Dunstan, and he does not look like a bread eater.
The moat is cold, green and full of Dunstan. Swimming in it would be a very bad idea.
You climb down the bank and slide into the moat. Dunstan has been waiting all morning for something to happen, and now it has.
Thornwall Castle is gray, patched and mostly upright. Smoke rises from the crooked kitchen chimney on the wall.
The gate stands open at the far end of the drawbridge. King Brannoc's great hall lies beyond it.
The drawbridge is down. It creaks, but it has creaked for years.
Green water circles the castle. Two yellow eyes drift along the surface.
PLEASE DO NOT FEED DUNSTAN, in the cook's handwriting.
Smoke rises from the crooked kitchen chimney. The cook is baking again.
A red pennant flies from the west tower. The side that faces the sun has faded to pink.
The road runs east into the meadow and on into the countryside.
You stop at the edge of the road. You have not answered the king's notice yet.
The king is in the great hall, across the drawbridge.
There are no herons here. Only Dunstan, and he is not a bird.
The notice says the Bell sank in the river gorge. Nobody has heard it ring since.
An ember that never goes out. The notice does not say who has it.
The notice says the Map will not stay in one place. That seems unhelpful in a map.
An old tree stump by the road. The cook uses it as a shelf.
A quill on a string, for signing the notice.
The last candle burns in the great hall. The notice says it is burning low.
There is no one here to give it to, except Dunstan.
It is broad daylight. Save the lantern for somewhere dark.
You don't have any bread.
Pale blue, with one small cloud of kitchen smoke.
The cook is inside, baking. Her smoke is all you can see of her.
Walk across the drawbridge and through the gate.
There is no more bread here.
The basket on the stump is empty now.
There is no one here to talk to except Dunstan.
The lantern is gone from its hook. You have it.

startMessages: Thornwall's gate stands open. A royal notice hangs beside the road; bread and a lit brass lantern wait on the bench. The hall lies north across the drawbridge, and the meadow road runs east. An alligator watches from the moat.

BY ORDER OF KING BRANNOC
Bring home the underwater Bell, the undying Ember and the wandering Map before our last candle fails.
Any squire may accept the errand. Journey supplies are on the bench.
The notice has a turned corner.
Behind the turned corner is a note from the cook: 'Polish the lantern with your sleeve. The stove salamander likes a face it can admire.'
Wenna signs beneath the royal seal. The king's errand is hers: find the Three Bright Things and bring them home.
Your name is already beneath the seal.
The loaf is yours for the journey. A heron calls from the meadow.
The bread is already in your satchel.
The brass lantern is warm. Its little flame holds steady.
You already carry the lantern.
The lantern's brass is dull, but its flame is sound. A loose sleeve would polish it nicely.
You polish the brass with your sleeve until your face appears in it.
The brass already shines. The flame needs no tending.
Take the lantern from the bench first.
The loaf smells of barley. It would make a good gift for a hungry bird.
The alligator floats very still. Its eyes follow your boots. The drawbridge is the safe way across.
The alligator turns toward you. Swimming here would put you straight into its jaws. You stay on the bank.
You leave the safe bank and swim toward the alligator. It reaches you before the bridge does.
The king is in the hall, across the drawbridge. His notice can commission you here.
The meadow road runs east. A heron waits beyond the rise.
The drawbridge is sound. Walk north between its rails to reach the hall.
The lantern is already lit. Keep its flame for the roadside candles.
The alligator has eaten. It is watching you out of professional interest. Save the bread for the heron.
The notice must stay for the other squires.
The heron's call comes from the meadow to the east.
The Bell, Ember and Map belong on the king's table. His notice names all three.
Read the royal notice, accept the errand, or take the bread and lantern. The hall is north across the bridge; the meadow road is east.
The bread would be better shared with someone hungry.
Your face shines in the polished brass. The salamander might enjoy its own reflection.
The old boundary stone marks the edge of the castle road.
The loaf has already gone to a good home.
